cards.context: Eno and Cale's only studio album together (Opal / Warner Bros., 1990).
cards.headline: Eno's first song album in 13 years
cards.snippet: Wrong Way Up is the sole collaborative studio album by Brian Eno and John Cale, released on 5 October 1990. It grew out of Cale's Words for the Dying, where the two co-wrote a song together for the first time — an experience Eno counted among the only really enjoyable parts of that record. Pitchfork notes it marks Eno's first song album since Before and After Science in 1977: Cale, sensing Eno growing comfortable with vocal songs again, proposed the full collaboration.

cards.context: Track 6 on Wrong Way Up; Eno sings lead, Robert Ahwai plays rhythm guitar.
cards.headline: Written alone, on a rhythm track made before Cale arrived
cards.snippet: Eno prepared this song before Cale arrived. He spent a couple of weeks in the studio making rhythm tracks — percussion tracks, really — and 'Spinning Away' was one of five songs built on them; he also wrote it completely alone, as he did 'Lay My Love' and 'The River'. Pitchfork hears it as collisions of speed: a rolling, off-balance rhythmic base over which Eno's vocals and Nell Catchpole's violin, playing in a different time signature, bob like boats. Its spinning image, 'like the night sky at Arles', casts Eno as Van Gogh painting The Starry Night.

cards.context: Recorded April–July 1990 at Eno's Wilderness Studio, Woodbridge, Suffolk; produced by Eno, co-produced by Cale.
cards.headline: Cabin fever, a chopstick, and a tour that never happened
cards.snippet: They admitted in promo interviews that they had not gotten on much of the time: Eno reportedly called Cale irrational, and Eno himself called the mood 'cabin fever' — two only children made to play together by their parents. It peaked when Cale turned to see an angry Eno coming towards him, a chopstick clenched in his hand: 'Imagine, being frightened by Brian Eno!' Cale complained that Eno kept changing the mix after he left, and that he had reneged on touring the album. The cover — giant playing cards, their heads at dagger points — came from the set design of that tour that never was.

cards.context: The song's only commercially significant cover; the original is not in the film, this is.
cards.headline: Sugar Ray, of all bands, for The Beach
cards.snippet: In 2000, the 'Fly' hitmakers covered the song for Danny Boyle's film The Beach, on a soundtrack Eno himself consulted on. They played it straight — shimmering synth strings where their own hits had ad-libs and vinyl scratches — and Pitchfork calls it 'a song so lovely that even a cover by Sugar Ray couldn't ruin it.' It sits at track 6 of the soundtrack, between Moby and New Order.
